title: Refreshing the Voting Portal cache is what starts the Ecosystem Spell Validation window
content:
A.1.10.2.4.11.2.4 requires the Governance Point to refresh the Voting Portal cache, "ensur[ing] that the executive corresponding to the new Spell is displayed promptly, **marking the start of the Ecosystem Spell Validation window**." It adds: "If required, Jetstream can provide the Governance Point with the necessary password to execute this action."

A formal governance period — the window in which Ecosystem Validators examine the Spell — therefore begins when a cache is manually refreshed, not when the Spell is deployed, the document merged, or a timestamp reached. The trigger is an operational side effect rather than a clock.

There is a defensible logic to it: the window should start when validators can actually *see* the proposal, and cache-refresh is the moment visibility becomes real. Tying the timer to publication-in-fact rather than publication-in-principle avoids a window that runs while nobody can read the thing being validated.

But it makes a governance deadline depend on a credential the Governance Point may not hold. If the refresh is late, the validation window starts late and compresses everything after it; if it is unclear exactly when the refresh happened, the window's start is ambiguous — and the Atlas records no timestamp for it, unlike the UTC deadlines that govern every other step in this process.

The pattern is worth noting more generally: several Atlas timings are anchored to human actions in third-party systems (Slack notifications, GitHub merges, cache refreshes) rather than to verifiable on-chain or documented events. Each such anchor is a small dependency of formal governance on operational access.
description: A.1.10.2.4.11.2.4 ties a formal governance timer to a manual operational action whose password may have to be obtained from another party.
